title: construction, views, and nets of 3D objects

lesson.title: Box Views & Nets – Flat Patterns That Fold Into 3D

steps.say: Okay, picture this. You want to build a little box to keep your phone charger, your earbuds, and that spare USB cable from getting lost in your backpack. Before you grab a craft knife and some cardstock, you need to figure out two things. First: what does the box look like from the top, the front, and the side? Those are called VIEWS. Second: what does the FLAT piece of cardboard look like before you cut and fold it? That flat pattern is called a NET. Today we are learning how to read, draw, and match both of those for rectangular boxes.

visual.caption: A 10 cm by 6 cm by 4 cm storage box

steps.say: Let's start with the views. Imagine you are standing right in front of your box. The face you see is the FRONT. You tilt your head and look down from above: that is the TOP view. You walk around to the side: that is the SIDE view. For our box, which is ten centimetres long, six centimetres wide, and four centimetres tall, here is what you see. The front view is a rectangle ten by four, because you see the length and the height. The top view is ten by six, because you see the length and the width. The side view is six by four, because you see the width and the height. Three simple rectangles, each one showing a single flat face of the box.

visual.caption: Front = 10 by 4, Top = 10 by 6, Side = 6 by 4

steps.say: Now here is the really fun part. If you carefully cut along the edges of that box and lay every single face flat on the table, you get a NET. Think of it like the flat instruction sheet that comes inside a cardboard model kit. For a rectangular box, the net always has exactly six rectangles. The front and the back are the same size. The top and the bottom are the same size. The two side faces are the same size. In our diagram, opposite faces share the same colour so your eyes can match them up instantly. When you fold along the lines, those six flat rectangles pop right back into a three-dimensional box.

visual.caption: The flat net: six rectangles, opposite faces same colour

steps.say: Let's do a quick worked example so this sticks. Suppose your charger box is eight centimetres long, five centimetres wide, and three centimetres tall. I want you to tell me the three views. Top view: you look down and see the length and the width, so that is eight by five. Front view: you see the length and the height, so eight by three. Side view: you see the width and the height, so five by three. Now the net: you need two rectangles of eight by five for the top and bottom, two of eight by three for the front and back, and two of five by three for the left and right sides. Cut those six pieces, tape them along the edges, and boom, you have a working little box. Simple, right?

visual.caption: Net for an 8 by 5 by 3 cm box

steps.say: Now let's level up a little bit. Think of a bentwood box or a lidded basket, the kind you might find at a BC craft fair in the summer. It is still a rectangular box, say twelve centimetres long, eight centimetres wide, and five centimetres tall, but one of those top faces is a LID that folds over the top. The net is almost the same six-rectangle pattern, but that top rectangle is slightly wider so it overlaps and acts as a cover. Your front view is still twelve by five, your side view is still eight by five, and your top view is twelve by eight. The key skill here is: when someone hands you a net and asks, can this fold into that box? You check that opposite faces match in size and that the overall dimensions work out.

visual.caption: Net for a lidded box: 12 by 8 by 5 cm

steps.say: Here is a mistake that trips up a lot of Grade 8 students, so listen carefully. When you are matching a net to a solid, always check that opposite faces are the same size AND that they are actually across from each other in the flat pattern. In our ten-by-six-by-four box, the two ten-by-six faces must be opposite, the two ten-by-four faces must be opposite, and the two six-by-four faces must be opposite. If a net you are looking at has two ten-by-six rectangles sitting right next to each other, it will NOT fold into our box, even though all six rectangles are the correct sizes. Always check position, not just size.

visual.caption: Check: opposite faces same size AND across from each other

steps.say: So here is your one-line takeaway. Views are the flat snapshots you see from the top, front, and side of a 3-D box, and a net is the flat, six-rectangle pattern that folds back up into that same box. Master reading and drawing those, and you can build anything from a tiny charger box to a proper bentwood lidded basket. You have got this.

visual.caption: From flat net to 3-D box: views and nets are two sides of the same idea

lesson.answer: A view is one flat face of a 3-D box seen from the top, front, or side; a net is the flat six-rectangle pattern that folds back into that box. Opposite faces must match in size and sit across from each other in the net.

practice.question: Your friend is making a small storage box for a BC Lions keychain, a spare pen, and a pack of gum. The box is 6 cm long, 4 cm wide, and 2 cm tall. (a) Describe the top, front, and side views. (b) List the six rectangles that make up the net, naming which pairs are opposite.
practice.answer: (a) Top view: 6 cm by 4 cm. Front view: 6 cm by 2 cm. Side view: 4 cm by 2 cm. (b) The net has two 6 by 4 rectangles (top and bottom, opposite each other), two 6 by 2 rectangles (front and back, opposite each other), and two 4 by 2 rectangles (left and right sides, opposite each other).
